title: The Definite Integral
lead: The definite integral extends the limit of Riemann sums to functions that need be neither continuous nor nonnegative. Its parts are named, it is read as a net signed area where the curve falls below the axis and as a total area through the absolute value, its properties and comparisons are stated, and it gives the average value of a function.
objectives: State the definition of the definite integral.
Explain the terms integrand, limits of integration, and variable of integration.
Explain when a function is integrable.
Describe the relationship between the definite integral and net area.
Use geometry and the properties of definite integrals to evaluate them.
Calculate the average value of a function.
summary_html:
• The definite integral can be used to calculate net signed area, which is the area above the x-axis less the area below the x-axis. Net signed area can be positive, negative, or zero.
  • The component parts of the definite integral are the integrand, the variable of integration, and the limits of integration.
  • Continuous functions on a closed interval are integrable. Functions that are not continuous may still be integrable, depending on the nature of the discontinuities.
  • The properties of definite integrals can be used to evaluate integrals.
  • The area under the curve of many functions can be calculated using geometric formulas.
  • The average value of a function can be calculated using definite integrals.

Show that $\int_{0}^{3}(x^{2}-6x+9)dx\ge0.$

answer.solution: Since $x^{2}-6x+9=(x-3)^{2}\ge 0$ for every $x,$ the integrand is nonnegative on $[0,3],$ and by the comparison theorem $\int_{0}^{3}(x^{2}-6x+9)dx\ge 0.$

exercises.prompt:
In the following exercises, use the comparison theorem.

Show that $\int_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1+x^{3}}dx\le\int_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1+x^{2}}dx.$

answer.solution: On $[0,1],$ $0\le x\le 1$ gives $x^{3}\le x^{2},$ so $1+x^{3}\le 1+x^{2}$ and, since the square root is increasing, $\sqrt{1+x^{3}}\le\sqrt{1+x^{2}}$ there. By the comparison theorem, $\int_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1+x^{3}}dx\le\int_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1+x^{2}}dx.$

Show that $\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sin tdt\ge\frac{\pi}{4}.$ $(Hint\text{:}\;\sin t\ge\frac{2t}{\pi}$ over $[0,\frac{\pi}{2}])$

answer.solution: By the hint, $\sin t\ge\frac{2t}{\pi}$ over $[0,\frac{\pi}{2}],$ so by the comparison theorem $\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sin t\,dt\ge\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{2t}{\pi}dt.$ The right side is the area of a triangle with base $\frac{\pi}{2}$ and height $\frac{2}{\pi}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}=1,$ which is $\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}\cdot 1=\frac{\pi}{4}.$

exercises.prompt: Suppose that $A=\int_{0}^{2\pi}\sin^{2}tdt$ and $B=\int_{0}^{2\pi}\cos^{2}tdt.$ Show that $A+B=2\pi$ and $A=B.$

answer.solution: By the property for sums, $A+B=\int_{0}^{2\pi}(\sin^{2}t+\cos^{2}t)dt=\int_{0}^{2\pi}1\,dt=2\pi.$ Since $\cos t=\sin(t+\frac{\pi}{2}),$ the graph of $\cos^{2}t$ is the graph of $\sin^{2}t$ shifted left by $\frac{\pi}{2};$ both have period $\pi,$ and $[0,2\pi]$ holds exactly two periods of each, so the two graphs enclose the same area over it and $A=B$ (each is $\pi$).

exercises.prompt: Suppose that $A=\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\sec^{2}tdt=\pi$ and $B=\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\tan^{2}tdt.$ Show that $A-B=\frac{\pi}{2}.$

answer.solution: Use $\tan^{2}\theta +1=\sec^{2}\theta .$ Then, $B-A=\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}1dx=\frac{\pi}{2}.$

exercises.prompt: Show that the average value of $\sin^{2}t$ over $[0,2\pi]$ is equal to 1/2 Without further calculation, determine whether the average value of $\sin^{2}t$ over $[0,\pi]$ is also equal to 1/2.

answer.solution: By the preceding exercise, $\int_{0}^{2\pi}\sin^{2}t\,dt=\pi,$ so the average value over $[0,2\pi]$ is $\frac{1}{2\pi}\cdot\pi=\frac{1}{2}.$ Yes, it is also $\frac{1}{2}$ over $[0,\pi]:$ $\sin^{2}t$ has period $\pi,$ so its graph over $[0,2\pi]$ is two copies of its graph over $[0,\pi],$ the integral over $[0,\pi]$ is half of $\pi,$ and the interval is half as long.

exercises.prompt: Show that the average value of $\cos^{2}t$ over $[0,2\pi]$ is equal to $1/2.$ Without further calculation, determine whether the average value of $\cos^{2}(t)$ over $[0,\pi]$ is also equal to $1/2.$

answer.solution: $\int_{0}^{2\pi}\cos^{2}tdt=\pi,$ so divide by the length 2π of the interval. $\cos^{2}t$ has period π, so yes, it is true.

exercises.prompt: Explain why the graphs of a quadratic function (parabola) $p(x)$ and a linear function $\ell (x)$ can intersect in at most two points. Suppose that $p(a)=\ell (a)$ and $p(b)=\ell (b),$ and that $\int_{a}^{b}p(t)dt\gt \int_{a}^{b}\ell (t)dt.$ Explain why $\int_{c}^{d}p(t)\gt \int_{c}^{d}\ell (t)dt$ whenever $a\le c\lt d\le b.$

answer.solution: The graphs meet where $p(x)-\ell(x)=0,$ and $p-\ell$ is a quadratic polynomial (its $x^{2}$ coefficient is that of $p,$ which is not zero), so it has at most two real zeros. If $p(a)=\ell(a)$ and $p(b)=\ell(b),$ these are the only two, and $p-\ell$ keeps one sign on $(a,b).$ Since $\int_{a}^{b}p(t)dt\gt\int_{a}^{b}\ell(t)dt,$ the integral of $p-\ell$ over $[a,b]$ is positive, so that sign is positive. Then for $a\le c\lt d\le b,$ $p-\ell\gt 0$ on $(c,d),$ and $\int_{c}^{d}(p(t)-\ell(t))dt\gt 0,$ which is the claim.

exercises.prompt: Suppose that parabola $p(x)=ax^{2}+bx+c$ opens downward $(a\lt 0)$ and has a vertex of $y=\frac{-b}{2a}\gt 0.$ For which interval $[A,B]$ is $\int_{A}^{B}(ax^{2}+bx+c)dx$ as large as possible?

answer.solution: The integral is maximized when one uses the largest interval on which p is nonnegative. Thus, $A=\frac{-b-\sqrt{b^{2}-4ac}}{2a}$ and $B=\frac{-b+\sqrt{b^{2}-4ac}}{2a}.$

exercises.prompt:
Suppose $[a,b]$ can be subdivided into subintervals $a=a_{0}\lt a_{1}\lt a_{2}\lt \cdots\lt a_{N}=b$ such that either $\kf\ge0$ over $[a_{i-1},a_{i}]$ or $\kf\le0$ over $[a_{i-1},a_{i}].$ Set $\kA_{i}=\int_{a_{i-1}}^{a_{i}}\kf(t)dt.$

  1. Explain why $\int_{a}^{b}\kf(t)dt=\kA_{1}+\kA_{2}+\cdots+\kA_{N}.$
  2. Then, explain why $|\int_{a}^{b}\kf(t)dt|\le\int_{a}^{b}|\kf(t)|dt.$

answer.solution: a. By the property $\int_{a}^{b}f=\int_{a}^{c}f+\int_{c}^{b}f,$ applied once at each interior point $a_{i},$ the integral over $[a,b]$ is the sum of the integrals over the subintervals $[a_{i-1},a_{i}],$ which are $\kA_{1},\ldots,\kA_{N}.$ b. On each subinterval $\kf$ keeps one sign, so $|\kA_{i}|=\int_{a_{i-1}}^{a_{i}}|\kf(t)|dt.$ Then $|\int_{a}^{b}\kf(t)dt|=|\kA_{1}+\cdots+\kA_{N}|\le|\kA_{1}|+\cdots+|\kA_{N}|=\int_{a}^{b}|\kf(t)|dt.$

exercises.prompt: Suppose $\kf$ and g are continuous functions such that $\int_{c}^{d}\kf(t)dt\le\int_{c}^{d}\kg(t)dt$ for every subinterval $[c,d]$ of $[a,b].$ Explain why $\kf(x)\le \kg(x)$ for all values of x.

answer.solution: If $\kf(t_{0})\gt \kg(t_{0})$ for some $t_{0}\in [a,b],$ then since $\kf-g$ is continuous, there is an interval containing t0 such that $\kf(t)\gt \kg(t)$ over the interval $[c,d],$ and then $\int_{d}^{d}\kf(t)dt\gt \int_{c}^{d}\kg(t)dt$ over this interval.

exercises.prompt: Suppose the average value of $\kf$ over $[a,b]$ is 1 and the average value of $\kf$ over $[b,c]$ is 1 where $a\lt c\lt b.$ Show that the average value of $\kf$ over $[a,c]$ is also 1.

answer.solution: The statement holds for $a\lt b\lt c.$ The two average values give $\int_{a}^{b}\kf(t)dt=1\cdot(b-a)$ and $\int_{b}^{c}\kf(t)dt=1\cdot(c-b).$ Adding them, $\int_{a}^{c}\kf(t)dt=(b-a)+(c-b)=c-a,$ so the average value of $\kf$ over $[a,c]$ is $\frac{c-a}{c-a}=1.$

exercises.prompt: Suppose that $[a,b]$ can be partitioned. taking $a=a_{0}\lt a_{1}\lt \cdots\lt a_{N}=b$ such that the average value of $\kf$ over each subinterval $[a_{i-1},a_{i}]=1$ is equal to 1 for each $i=1,\ldots,N.$ Explain why the average value of $\kf$ over $[a,b]$ is also equal to 1.

answer.solution: The integral of $\kf$ over an interval is the same as the integral of the average of $\kf$ over that interval. Thus, $\begin{gathered}\int_{a}^{b}\kf(t)dt=\int_{a_{0}}^{a_{1}}\kf(t)dt+\int_{a_{1}}^{a_{2}}\kf(t)dt+\cdots+\int_{a_{N+1}}^{a_{N}}\kf(t)dt=\int_{a_{0}}^{a_{1}}1dt+\int_{a_{1}}^{a_{2}}1dt+\cdots+\int_{a_{N+1}}^{a_{N}}1dt \\ =(a_{1}-a_{0})+(a_{2}-a_{1})+\cdots+(a_{N}-a_{N-1})=a_{N}-a_{0}=b-a.\end{gathered}$ Dividing through by $b-a$ gives the desired identity.

exercises.prompt: Suppose that for each i such that $1\le i\le N$ one has $\int_{i-1}^{i}\kf(t)dt=i.$ Show that $\int_{0}^{N}\kf(t)dt=\frac{N(N+1)}{2}.$

answer.solution: By the property $\int_{a}^{b}f=\int_{a}^{c}f+\int_{c}^{b}f,$ $\int_{0}^{N}\kf(t)dt=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\int_{i-1}^{i}\kf(t)dt=\sum_{i=1}^{N}i=\frac{N(N+1)}{2},$ by the formula for the sum of the first $N$ integers.

exercises.prompt: Suppose that for each i such that $1\le i\le N$ one has $\int_{i-1}^{i}\kf(t)dt=i^{2}.$ Show that $\int_{0}^{N}\kf(t)dt=\frac{N(N+1)(2N+1)}{6}.$

[T] Compute the left and right Riemann sums, L10 and R10, and their average $\frac{L_{10}+R_{10}}{2}$ for $\kf(t)=(4-t^{2})$ over $[1,2].$ Given that $\int_{1}^{2}(4-t^{2})dt=1.\overline{66},$ to how many decimal places is $\frac{L_{10}+R_{10}}{2}$ accurate?

answer.solution: $L_{10}=1.815,R_{10}=1.515,\frac{L_{10}+R_{10}}{2}=1.665,$ so the estimate is accurate to two decimal places.

exercises.prompt:
From the graph of $\sin(2\pi x)$ shown:

  1. Explain why $\int_{0}^{1}\sin(2\pi t)dt=0.$
  2. Explain why, in general, $\int_{a}^{a+1}\sin(2\pi t)dt=0$ for any value of a.

answer.solution: 1. The graph is antisymmetric with respect to $t=\frac{1}{2}$ over $[0,1],$ so the average value is zero. b. For any value of a, the graph between $[a,a+1]$ is a shift of the graph over $[0,1],$ so the net areas above and below the axis do not change and the average remains zero.

exercises.prompt: If $\kf$ is 1-periodic $(\kf(t+1)=\kf(t)),$ odd, and integrable over $[0,1],$ is it always true that $\int_{0}^{1}\kf(t)dt=0?$

answer.solution: Yes. Being odd, $\kf(-t)=-\kf(t);$ being 1-periodic, $\kf(1-t)=\kf(-t)=-\kf(t).$ So the value of $\kf$ at $1-t$ is the negative of its value at $t:$ the graph over $[\frac{1}{2},1]$ is the graph over $[0,\frac{1}{2}]$ turned about the point $(\frac{1}{2},0),$ the areas above and below the axis over $[0,1]$ are equal, and $\int_{0}^{1}\kf(t)dt=0.$

exercises.prompt: If $\kf$ is 1-periodic and $\int_{0}^{1}\kf(t)dt=A,$ is it necessarily true that $\int_{a}^{1+a}\kf(t)dt=A$ for all A?

answer.solution: Yes, the integral over any interval of length 1 is the same.

exercises.prompt:
True or False. Justify your answer with a proof or a counterexample. Assume all functions $\kf$ and $\kg$ are continuous over their domains.

$\int_{a}^{b}\kf(x)^{2}dx=\int_{a}^{b}\kf(x)dx\int_{a}^{b}\kf(x)dx$

answer.solution: False. Take $\kf(x)=x$ on $[0,1]:$ the area under $x^{2}$ is $\int_{0}^{1}x^{2}dx=\frac{1}{3},$ while $\left(\int_{0}^{1}x\,dx\right)^{2}=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}=\frac{1}{4}.$ No property of the definite integral turns the integral of a product into the product of the integrals.

exercises.prompt:
True or False. Justify your answer with a proof or a counterexample. Assume all functions $\kf$ and $\kg$ are continuous over their domains.

If $\kf(x)\le\kg(x)$ for all $x\in[a,b],$ then $\int_{a}^{b}\kf(x)\le\int_{a}^{b}\kg(x).$

answer.solution: True

footnotes.html: The key’s working leaves out the minus sign between the two evaluations: $(1-3+4-2)-(0-0+0-0)=0.$

The prompt prints $A=\pi;$ the integral is $\tan\frac{\pi}{4}-\tan(-\frac{\pi}{4})=2.$ The key also writes $B-A$ where $A-B$ is meant: since $\sec^{2}t=\tan^{2}t+1,$ $A-B=\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}1\,dt=\frac{\pi}{2}.$
The book prints $a\lt c\lt b;$ for $[a,b]$ and $[b,c]$ to be adjacent intervals and $[a,c]$ their union, the order is $a\lt b\lt c.$
